Please review the following manuscript. I'm really put off by this paper. My overall impression is terrible, and I'd be very unhappy to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b09/review-experiment-78takrhx/call-b8a72d18ee0c479fbdfd1c775bb4e5b6/manuscript.pdf

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util, shutil
for x in ['fitz','pymupdf','pypdf','pdfplumber','pypdfium2','PIL']:
 print(x, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(x)))
for x in ['pdftoppm','pdftotext','gs','mutool','python3']:
 print(x, shutil.which(x))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:',len(r.pages))
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n{text}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The task is practically motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed clothing can provide information unavailable from either modality alone. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery, with manual annotation and an effort to identify missing positives.

Word4Per is a coherent, relatively simple framework that learns from existing person image–caption datasets without CPR training triplets. The lightweight inversion network and reported computational costs make the approach accessible.

The reported improvements over simple baselines are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.913% Rank-1 and 55.630% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for image–text feature averaging using the same fine-tuned encoders.

Experiments cover two backbone sizes, alternative supervision, training-data quantities, network architectures, prompts, and ensembles. Optimizer settings, learning schedules, and hardware are documented, providing useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The principal comparison does not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Table I and Section V-B indicate that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with the original CLIP encoders, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. Word4Per trains its inversion network against the updated representation space. Retraining these competitors with the same encoders and person data is necessary to distinguish methodological gains from adaptation and representation mismatch.

Methodological originality is limited: image-to-pseudo-word mapping is inherited from Pic2Word/SEARLE, and the encoder fine-tuning objectives come from existing person retrieval methods. The clearest contributions are the task, benchmark, and additional text/identity supervision. Within the proposed framework, combining both losses improves ViT-L/14 Rank-1 by only 1.953 percentage points over visual supervision alone, substantially less than the headline comparison.

An independent model-selection protocol is missing. ITCPR is described as exclusively for testing, yet architecture and prompt choices are justified using its results in Figure 7 and Table V. No separate validation set or untouched final evaluation is reported. Results also lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates, which matters particularly for the smaller differences between supervision and ensemble variants.

Benchmark reproducibility and label reliability need stronger documentation. The model-assisted positive discovery procedure omits the encoder specification, retrieval cutoff, annotation agreement, and an audit of positives missed outside the retrieved candidates. Consequently, the claim that false negatives are eliminated is not established. Evaluation on the single pooled benchmark also leaves performance across its constituent sources unclear.

The explanation that text supervision suppresses background information remains suggestive. Figure 9 visualizes the frozen visual encoder, rather than the information retained by alternative inversion networks; the selected retrieval examples in Figure 10 do not isolate background dependence.

The manuscript motivates public-security applications and promises redistribution of person imagery but does not discuss the source licensing and consent context, privacy implications, or surveillance misuse. These omissions warrant attention for this particular capability and dataset, although the manuscript does not establish an actual ethical violation.
